display_name: DOJ/FTC Antitrust Guidelines for International Enforcement and Cooperation (2017): the FTAIA and import, non-import and U.S.-government commerce, comity, foreign government involvement, and cooperation with foreign authorities, as what the agencies say they will do. Agency enforcement policy, not law.
seat: a business or person engaged in international activities, with counsel, asking what the agencies say they will do with its conduct; for chapter 5, also the person who produced information to the agencies. No seat layer is written (deferred).
scope: AGENCY ENFORCEMENT POLICY, NOT LAW: results say what the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission (or the Department alone, or the FSIA or a statute as the 2017 text summarises it) say, keeping each sentence's modal and speaker, never what is lawful. The text replaces the 1995 Antitrust Enforcement Guidelines for International Operations (read at source, [pdf page 4]; the 1995 text not read). Encoded: chapter 2's tests only (2, 2.2, 2.4, 2.7, 2.8, 2.9, 2.12; F28); chapter 3: how the FTAIA bears on each statute, import commerce (3.1, F1), the kind of commerce (F2), what the FTAIA does, the three-valued findings of a direct, substantial and reasonably foreseeable effect (F5, F8), 'gives rise to' by kind of claim (F3), the effects exception with Section 6a's export-only limit (F19), what the agencies do (F4), the private damages sentences (F24), n.80, n.93 and n.82's courts' readings reported, never resolved (F13), n.100, and U.S. government financing or purchasing (3.3, F6); 4.1's comity considerations as a report that weighs nothing (F9), when no conflict of law exists (F7) and a foreign authority's action; 4.2.1 to 4.2.4 (F10, F11, F12, F14, F26); chapter 5's sentences on what the agencies may, will, will not or cannot do (F16): cooperation by the state of the investigations, compelled production, blocking statutes, Second Requests, sharing by kind of information with waivers and understandings (F17, F18) and the IAEAA's HSR exclusion, privileged and waived information from a foreign authority, remedies reaching outside the United States, grand jury secrecy and leniency (F27). Inputs, never computed: every finding the text leaves to the agencies or a court. Answers NOTHING where the text states no outcome. Not encoded: chapter 1, the statutes' prohibitions and penalties, dated figures (HSR thresholds, the 2016 penalty limit, ACPERA's 2020 sunset), foreign law, 5.1.2, the descriptive parts of chapter 5, Example H, Annex 1.

forks.F1: 3.1: conduct itself involves import commerce when the participants sell in or for delivery to the United States, provide closely connected services, or the agencies so find; their own importing, acting as importers, direction and share decide nothing
forks.F2: import commerce wins over export; non-import commerce is export or wholly foreign
forks.F3: 'gives rise to': the qualifying effect itself for the agencies' equitable and the Department's criminal actions; an adverse effect that proximately caused the injury for damages (private and Section 4A)
forks.F4: a circumstance of a sufficient connection is import commerce or the effects exception met, 'if the agencies so determine'; a private claim and domestic conduct are NOTHING; 3.3 is separate
forks.F6: 3.3: the two exclusions are read first; the forms the involvement 'could include' are NOTHING without a substantial portion
forks.F7: 4.1: neutral foreign law, then compliance with both, then n.144's blocking statute; otherwise a conflict of law exists (the 'if' read with its converse)
forks.F8: the FTAIA findings are MAYBE BOOLEAN: not yet determined, found to hold, found not to hold
forks.F9: 4.1's comity considerations are reported, never weighed
forks.F10: n.112's 'include' is open: an entity outside the definition is NOTHING; an individual official is FALSE; a state-owned enterprise is a majority-owned instrumentality
forks.F11: 4.2.2 with every criterion met: Example E's 'would acknowledge a defense of sovereign compulsion'
forks.F12: 4.2.2: compelled conduct in a third country, alone, is NOTHING ('generally')
forks.F13: the courts' differing readings (n.80, n.82, n.93) are reported values, never inputs
forks.F14: 4.2.4: genuine is not a sham; a sham before a U.S. entity, or a case where Noerr-Pennington would not apply there, is NOTHING
forks.F15: 5.1.1's 'may compel ... when' is sufficient only: a failed condition is NOTHING
forks.F16: a rule in chapter 5 is a sentence saying what the agencies or the Department may, will, will not or cannot do, or what required cooperation includes; practice descriptions are inert
forks.F17: four waiver states; a refusal is not a waiver never asked for
forks.F18: 5.1.4: a covering waiver with no understanding of confidentiality and no IAEAA route is NOTHING
forks.F19: the effects exception: one qualifying effect suffices; the export-only outcome needs every other effect found to fail; no effect named is not met
forks.F20: 2.7: notice, then scope of the notification, then the joint-production condition
forks.F21: 2.8: not filing alone is NOTHING; an association meeting no limit is within the exemption as the 2017 text describes it
forks.F22: 2.9: fraud first; a person not named, an activity not specified or non-complying conduct is outside the certificate
forks.F23: 2.12: a complying settlement within the authorized measures is NOTHING ('certain settlements')
forks.F24: 3.2's private damages sentences each on their own terms; otherwise NOTHING, the Section 4A claim included
forks.F25: 2.4 speaks only of a transaction not subject to the HSR Act; one that is subject is NOTHING
forks.F26: 4.2.1: a non-civil case and an entity outside the definition are NOTHING; no burden is invented
forks.F27: 5.2: a grand jury matter with an applicable exception is NOTHING
forks.F28: a test in chapter 2 is a sentence with a condition and an outcome the text itself states (eight parts); the statutes' prohibitions are inert; 2.5's ACPERA damages limit is a test left out because n.41 dates it (sunset 22 June 2020), not taken as a labelled input
forks.F29: contradictory inputs are read in a stated order (no foreign commerce first; an individual official first; fraud first; detail before ambiguity; neutral law first)
